hypothesis: The neuron is highly selective for repetitive, periodic vertical linear structures, primarily manifesting as parallel bars, slats, or pickets found in objects like cribs, fences, railings, and grilles. This selectivity extends to other rhythmic vertical arrangements or grids, such as the hanging handles of kitchen utensils, the vertical ridges of combination locks, and the vertical segments of digital 7-segment numerals. The activating features are typically monochromatic and distinct, appearing as either bright elements (white, silver, cream) or dark forms (black, deep brown, forest green) that create a sharp, high-contrast boundary against a background of opposing tone—commonly pitch black, dark blue, or deep shadow for light objects, and white, beige, or sage green for dark objects. The repetitive vertical features generally dominate the composition, typically spanning 50–100% of the vertical axis and repeating horizontally across the majority of the frame. The neuron remains invariant to object identity (furniture, architectural elements, electronics), material properties, and lighting direction, provided the distinct, alternating vertical geometry and strong figure-ground contrast are maintained.
